chunk_text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Egg allergy
  Synonyms:
    - Hen's egg allergy
    - IgE-mediated egg allergy
    - Type-1 hypersensitivity to egg
  Description: An adverse immunologic reaction to egg proteins, primarily ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and ovomucoid (Gal d 1), mediated by specific IgE antibodies. The reaction is typically immediate type-1 hypersensitivity with rapid symptom onset; late-phase and delayed hypersensitivity reactions can also occur, particularly in the context of eczema.
  Epidemiology: Prevalence is approximately 2% in children and 0.1% in adults in the United Kingdom. Onset most commonly occurs in infancy, often after the first apparent ingestion; new-onset egg allergy in adults is rare.
  Clinical presentation: Typical presentation is in infancy, with rapid onset (within minutes) of cutaneous symptoms (erythema, urticaria, angioedema) and/or vomiting following egg ingestion. Severe reactions are less common and may involve respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, breathing difficulty) or cardiovascular symptoms (pallor, floppiness). Reaction severity is influenced by the amount of egg ingested and the degree of cooking; raw egg white is the most allergenic form. Delayed worsening of eczema may also occur.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Childhood-onset egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Usually presents in infancy, often with mild to moderate symptoms; high rate of spontaneous resolution by adolescence; commonly associated with other atopic conditions such as eczema and asthma.
    - Name: Adult-onset egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Rare; may occur as new onset in adulthood after years of tolerance, or as persistence of childhood allergy; tends to be more severe and persistent; can be associated with bird-egg syndrome or occupational sensitization.
    - Name: Occupational egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Results from inhalation of egg protein aerosols in occupational settings (e.g., baking industry); may develop respiratory symptoms and subsequently react upon ingestion.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To establish a diagnosis of egg allergy based on typical symptoms.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected egg allergy.
      Interpretation: Rapid onset (minutes) of erythema, urticaria, angioedema, and/or vomiting after egg ingestion is highly suggestive. Mild reactions in a clear history are sufficient for diagnosis without further testing.
    - Test: Skin prick test (SPT) with standardized whole egg reagent
      Purpose: To confirm IgE sensitization to egg.
      When indicated: Moderate‑severe reactions, or when the clinical history is unclear.
      Interpretation: A weal size of ≥3 mm in combination with a supportive clinical history is diagnostic in most cases. Higher cut‑offs (e.g., ≥5 mm in children under 2 years) increase specificity. SPT weal size does not predict clinical severity. SPT should not be used for screening in the absence of suspected reaction.
    - Test: Egg‑specific IgE assay (serum)
      Purpose: To detect circulating egg‑specific IgE antibodies.
      When indicated: When SPT is unavailable, or in moderate‑severe cases to support diagnosis.
      Interpretation: No single diagnostic cut‑off value is applicable across all ages; low levels can be found in egg‑tolerant children. Therefore, results must be correlated with clinical history. Egg‑specific IgE should not be measured in asymptomatic individuals as it may lead to unnecessary dietary restriction.
    - Test: Component‑resolved diagnostics (specific IgE to Gal d 1, Gal d 2, Gal d 3, Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify sensitization to individual egg allergens, which aids in predicting persistence and tolerance to baked egg.
      When indicated: When assessing likelihood of resolution, especially in older children or adults; may guide decisions on oral food challenge.
      Interpretation: Sensitization to multiple components, particularly Gal d 1 (ovomucoid), suggests persistent allergy. Negative Gal d 1 IgE is associated with a higher chance of tolerating baked egg. Ovalbumin (Gal d 2) IgE is common but less predictive of severity. Gal d 5 indicates egg yolk allergy and possible bird‑egg syndrome.
    - Test: Oral food challenge (OFC)
      Purpose: To definitively confirm or refute the diagnosis, or to prove tolerance has developed.
      When indicated: When clinical history and test results are discordant, or to assess resolution of allergy. Hospital‑based challenges are reserved for high‑risk patients (Box 4).
      Interpretation: A controlled graded ingestion of egg (baked, lightly cooked, or raw) under medical supervision; positive if objective allergic symptoms occur. Baked egg challenges are used to determine if heat‑processed egg is tolerated.
    - Test: Prick‑to‑prick testing with raw egg
      Purpose: To detect sensitization to raw egg proteins.
      When indicated: Not routinely recommended; may be considered in research settings.
      Interpretation: A weal of ≥13 mm has been reported as diagnostic. Does not predict baked egg tolerance and carries a risk of systemic reaction; not standardized.
    - Test: Skin prick test with baked egg slurry
      Purpose: To predict the outcome of a baked egg challenge.
      When indicated: Research setting; not routinely used in clinical practice.
      Interpretation: High negative predictive value reported in one study.
    - Test: Peanut‑specific IgE (co‑testing)
      Purpose: To assess risk of peanut allergy and guide early peanut introduction advice.
      When indicated: Infants with moderate‑severe egg allergy.
      Interpretation: Egg allergy in infancy is associated with increased risk of peanut allergy; early peanut introduction may prevent its development.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Egg white‑specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Indicates sensitization to egg white proteins; supports clinical diagnosis when history is positive but not diagnostic in isolation.
    - Marker: Ovalbumin (Gal d 2) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Major heat‑labile egg white allergen; commonly detected in egg‑allergic individuals.
    - Marker: Ovomucoid (Gal d 1) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable or elevated
      Clinical significance: Heat‑stable and immunodominant allergen; sensitization is associated with persistent egg allergy, greater severity, and reduced likelihood of baked egg tolerance.
    - Marker: Gal d 3 specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Egg white allergen; may contribute to sensitization profile.
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Egg yolk allergen; marker for bird‑egg syndrome; indicates cross‑reactivity with bird feather allergens.
    - Marker: Skin prick test weal diameter (to egg white)
      Expected result: ≥3 mm
      Clinical significance: Supports diagnosis of egg allergy when combined with history; larger weals increase specificity but do not correlate with severity.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: Prognostic indicators for resolution of egg allergy
      Components:
      - Age at tolerance to baked egg
      - Reaction severity (mild/cutaneous only vs respiratory/multisystem)
      - Presence of asthma
      - Severity of eczema
      - Egg‑specific IgE level
      - Sensitization to multiple egg allergen components (especially ovomucoid/Gal d 1)
      - Number of co‑existing food allergies
      - Atopic comorbidities
      Risk groups:
      - Group: Favorable prognosis
      Criteria: Mild or cutaneous‑only initial reactions, no asthma, low egg‑specific IgE, early tolerance of baked egg, absence of ovomucoid or multi‑component sensitization, and no other food allergies or severe eczema.
      Expected outcome: High likelihood of outgrowing allergy; median age of resolution for well‑cooked egg is 67 months and for uncooked egg 127 months; approximately 68% resolve by 16 years.
      - Group: Unfavorable prognosis
      Criteria: History of respiratory or cardiovascular severe reactions, presence of asthma or severe eczema, high egg‑specific IgE, sensitization to multiple components (especially ovomucoid), and multiple food allergies.
      Expected outcome: More likely to have persistent allergy into adolescence or adulthood; delayed achievement of tolerance to well‑cooked egg and uncooked egg.
      Interpretation: These factors guide the timing and setting of egg reintroduction (home vs hospital) and the need for specialist allergy follow‑up. Children with favorable features may attempt home‑based baked egg introduction from 12 months.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: All infants and young children with egg allergy should be periodically assessed for suitability of reintroduction. Adults and older children with persistent egg allergy should be reviewed at intervals to update emergency medication training, repeat specific IgE testing, and consider component testing and oral food challenges to determine if resolution has occurred. Exact frequency is not specified but typically annual or as guided by clinical progress.
    Recommended tests:
      - Interval clinical history (new reactions, dietary adherence, growth)
      - Egg‑specific IgE (and possibly component IgE) to monitor sensitization trends
      - Skin prick testing when appropriate
      - Consideration of oral food challenge to baked egg or cooked egg when prognostic factors are favorable
    Long term effects:
      - Risk of accidental anaphylaxis, including fatalities
      - Dietary restrictions impacting quality of life and social participation
      - Psychosocial burden: anxiety, bullying, family stress
      - Potential for nutritional deficiencies if multiple food allergies
      - In persistent cases, lifelong egg avoidance may be required
    Survivorship notes: Many children outgrow egg allergy; early introduction of baked egg may accelerate tolerance. Adults with persistent allergy should receive ongoing support and education. All patients need an up‑to‑date emergency management plan and ready access to antihistamines and adrenaline auto‑injectors.

  Name: Bird‑egg syndrome

  Description: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.
  Epidemiology: Rare; described mainly in adults, particularly women, with prolonged exposure to budgerigars, pigeons, or other caged birds.
  Clinical presentation: Upper and lower respiratory symptoms (rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma) on inhalation of bird allergens; gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Symptoms are triggered by ingestion of egg yolk, which contains high concentrations of alpha‑livetin. Onset typically after years of bird exposure.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To identify the characteristic cross‑reactivity between bird and egg allergens.
      When indicated: Suspected cases with respiratory symptoms on bird exposure and food reactions to egg yolk.
      Interpretation: A history of bird feather sensitivity and symptoms with egg (especially yolk) or chicken meat is highly suggestive.
    - Test: Skin prick test or specific IgE to egg yolk
      Purpose: To confirm sensitization to egg yolk proteins.
      When indicated: When bird‑egg syndrome is suspected.
      Interpretation: Positive test indicates sensitization to yolk allergen; further distinction can be made with component testing.
    - Test: Specific IgE to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify the specific cross‑reactive allergen.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected bird‑egg syndrome.
      Interpretation: Elevated Gal d 5 IgE confirms the diagnosis.
    - Test: Skin prick test to bird feathers
      Purpose: To demonstrate sensitization to bird allergens.
      When indicated: When respiratory symptoms on bird exposure are present.
      Interpretation: Positive test supports the diagnosis of bird‑related respiratory allergy.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Diagnostic for bird‑egg syndrome; explains the cross‑reactivity between bird feather allergens and egg yolk.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Periodic specialist review, similar to adult egg allergy; frequency not defined. Repeat specific IgE testing and reassessment of bird avoidance measures.
    Recommended tests:
      - Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      - Spirometry if asthma symptoms present
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent allergy to egg yolk and bird feather allergens
      - Risk of anaphylaxis with egg yolk ingestion
      - Need for bird avoidance and egg‑free diet
    Survivorship notes: This syndrome tends to persist lifelong. Patients must carry emergency medications and avoid egg yolk and bird exposure.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Bird‑egg syndrome
  Synonyms:
    - Alpha‑livetin allergy
    - Egg yolk allergy with bird feather sensitization
  Description: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.
  Epidemiology: Rare; described mainly in adults, particularly women, with prolonged exposure to budgerigars, pigeons, or other caged birds.
  Clinical presentation: Upper and lower respiratory symptoms (rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma) on inhalation of bird allergens; gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Symptoms are triggered by ingestion of egg yolk, which contains high concentrations of alpha‑livetin. Onset typically after years of bird exposure.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To identify the characteristic cross‑reactivity between bird and egg allergens.
      When indicated: Suspected cases with respiratory symptoms on bird exposure and food reactions to egg yolk.
      Interpretation: A history of bird feather sensitivity and symptoms with egg (especially yolk) or chicken meat is highly suggestive.
    - Test: Skin prick test or specific IgE to egg yolk
      Purpose: To confirm sensitization to egg yolk proteins.
      When indicated: When bird‑egg syndrome is suspected.
      Interpretation: Positive test indicates sensitization to yolk allergen; further distinction can be made with component testing.
    - Test: Specific IgE to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify the specific cross‑reactive allergen.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected bird‑egg syndrome.
      Interpretation: Elevated Gal d 5 IgE confirms the diagnosis.
    - Test: Skin prick test to bird feathers
      Purpose: To demonstrate sensitization to bird allergens.
      When indicated: When respiratory symptoms on bird exposure are present.
      Interpretation: Positive test supports the diagnosis of bird‑related respiratory allergy.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Diagnostic for bird‑egg syndrome; explains the cross‑reactivity between bird feather allergens and egg yolk.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Periodic specialist review, similar to adult egg allergy; frequency not defined. Repeat specific IgE testing and reassessment of bird avoidance measures.
    Recommended tests:
      - Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      - Spirometry if asthma symptoms present
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent allergy to egg yolk and bird feather allergens
      - Risk of anaphylaxis with egg yolk ingestion
      - Need for bird avoidance and egg‑free diet
    Survivorship notes: This syndrome tends to persist lifelong. Patients must carry emergency medications and avoid egg yolk and bird exposure.

#### 6 | DIAGNOSIS

Acute clinical signs have usually resolved by the time the patient reaches medical attention. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg. Children with a clear history of a mild reaction to egg can be diagnosed and managed in a primary care setting without further testing. Only children with moderate-severe reactions, or where the history remains unclear, require further investigation to confirm and manage egg allergy. 7 | INVESTIGATIONS

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23.

7 | INVESTIGATIONS

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23. It is not standardized and there is a risk of severe reactions, so is not routinely recommended outside research settings. Skin prick testing using a slurry of baked egg had a high negative predictive value for a negative baked egg challenge in one study.24 It is not routinely used in clinical practice.

#### 6 | DIAGNOSIS

Acute clinical signs have usually resolved by the time the patient reaches medical attention. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg. Children with a clear history of a mild reaction to egg can be diagnosed and managed in a primary care setting without further testing. Only children with moderate-severe reactions, or where the history remains unclear, require further investigation to confirm and manage egg allergy. 7 | INVESTIGATIONS

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23. It is not standardized and there is a risk of severe reactions, so is not routinely recommended outside research settings.

#### 6 | DIAGNOSIS

Acute clinical signs have usually resolved by the time the patient reaches medical attention. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg. Children with a clear history of a mild reaction to egg can be diagnosed and managed in a primary care setting without further testing. Only children with moderate-severe reactions, or where the history remains unclear, require further investigation to confirm and manage egg allergy. 7 | INVESTIGATIONS

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23. It is not standardized and there is a risk of severe reactions, so is not routinely recommended outside research settings.

| |---| #### 9.4 | Home introduction of egg Home introduction is not the same as a food challenge. It aims to gradually introduce a food, to which a child previously reacted, back into the patient's diet. Egg is gradually introduced using a ladder (Figure 1), in a form less likely to cause an allergic reaction, at low amounts. The quantity and allergenicity are gradually increased as the child is able to tolerate it. This approach helps ensure safety with a view to promoting tolerance to more allergenic forms of the food. Children without asthma, or with well-controlled mild asthma, and who have had only mild cutaneous symptoms on significant exposure (e.g. a mouthful of lightly cooked egg) may try a small amount of baked egg (e.g. pea-sized piece of sponge cake) from the age of about 12 months at home (Appendix S3). If this is tolerated regularly, in good amounts, then gradual staged reintroduction of lightly cooked egg according to the egg ladder (Figure 1 and patient information leaflet Appendix S3) may be considered. Once baked egg is fully tolerated, it should be included 2–3 times per week. #### 7.3 | Egg component testing

The egg white components are ovomucoid (Gal d 1), ovalbumin (Gal d 2), ovotransferrin (Gal d 3), lysozyme (Gal d 4) and livetin (Gal d 5). Ovomucoid (Gal d 1) is heat stable and immunodominant.2,3 The role of component allergens in predicting tolerance to baked egg white, or resolution of egg allergy in routine clinical practice has yet to be established.24 Persisting egg allergy is associated with a positive Gal d 1, and a level ≥11 kU/L indicates a high risk of reacting to cooked and raw egg.3 Gal d 1 is also a good indicator of whether the child is allergic only to raw egg, or to both cooked and raw egg.26 The acquisition of tolerance to egg is associated with a decrease in IgE to egg white and Gal d 1.27 When using test results to identify children at a high risk of anaphylaxis, although egg white sIgE levels are more sensitive, Gal d 1 has better positive predictive value and specificity.28 The current evidence suggests that egg components are rarely needed for the routine diagnosis and management of egg allergy in children but can be a useful adjunct for the assessment of egg allergy resolution in adults (Box 2).

8 | MANAGEMENT

- 8.1 | Avoidance diets

Eggs served in a recognizable form are relatively easy to avoid. They are used as an ingredient of many manufactured foods; therefore, food labels must be consistently checked. Uncommon sources of egg include quorn, confectionary and egg hidden in a food, usually ‘egg free’, e.g., pizza dough. Extra care needs to be taken with foods sold loose (non-pre-packed) as there may be risk of cross-contamination. Individuals with severe egg allergy will need to completely avoid food sold loose/on buffets. All species of egg (e.g. quail/duck) are given the generic name ‘egg’ on a label. Verbal and written advice on avoidance of egg products should be provided (see Appendices S2 and S3).

Acute clinical signs have usually resolved by the time the patient reaches medical attention. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg. - 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. The treatment and management of ocular allergy (OA) remains a major concern for different specialties, including allergists, ophthalmologists, primary care physicians, rhinologists, pediatricians, dermatologists, clinical immunologists and pharmacists. We performed a systematic review of all relevant publications in Medline, SCOPUS and WebScience including systematic reviews and meta-analysis. Topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers or double action drugs are the first choice of treatment. All of them are effective in reducing signs and symptoms of OA. Introduction Ocular allergy (OA) represents a collection of ocular hypersensitivity disorders affecting the eyelid, conjunctiva and cornea. OA includes seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC), vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis (VKC and AKC) and contact blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC) (1). These clinical subtypes may be diagnosed and managed by ophthalmologists, allergists, pediatricians and rhinologists, with or without experience in managing allergies, considering clinical history and signs and symptoms, aided by in vivo and in vitro tests (1-3). Although several studies suggest a high co-morbidity of conjunctivitis and rhinitis, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians as a minor problem and sub-optimally treated. A recent survey revealed that daily treatment of OA has little concordance with current recommendations(4). Topical ocular decongestants and corticosteroids were used in the majority of cases. This was independent of the specific diagnosis of OA subtype and severity. Topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers, which

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature.

chunk_text:
Introduction Ocular allergy (OA) represents a collection of ocular hypersensitivity disorders affecting the eyelid, conjunctiva and cornea. OA includes seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC), vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis (VKC and AKC) and contact blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC) (1). These clinical subtypes may be diagnosed and managed by ophthalmologists, allergists, pediatricians and rhinologists, with or without experience in managing allergies, considering clinical history and signs and symptoms, aided by in vivo and in vitro tests (1-3). Although several studies suggest a high co-morbidity of conjunctivitis and rhinitis, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians as a minor problem and sub-optimally treated. A recent survey revealed that daily treatment of OA has little concordance with current recommendations(4). Topical ocular decongestants and corticosteroids were used in the majority of cases. This was independent of the specific diagnosis of OA subtype and severity. Topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers, which

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature.

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature. One important problem is that patients with ocular allergic disease often self-medicate; they purchase OTC medications and fail to seek help even when those therapies are ineffective [22, 23]. Conversely, the use and overuse of OTC products may lead to adverse effects such as rebound vasodilation [23]. Furthermore, BAK is a very

common preservative in these solutions – present in over 70% of OTC eye drops – that, as mentioned, has the potential to induce ocular toxicity and exacerbate ocular surface damage [7]. ## Is There Room for Improvement in the Management of AC? AC continues to be an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease [7]. Considering the need for differential diagnosis, a multidisciplinary approach involving allergists, general practitioners, otolaryngologists, and eye care specialists is advisable [1, 17]. It should be borne in mind that in many settings, allergic conjunctivitis patients are often seen in primary care and, when referred to a specialist, those with SAC symptoms are usually referred to the allergist, while patients with PAC are more often referred to the ophthalmologist for differential diagnosis [1]. ### Should Allergists Routinely Investigate Hypersensitivity Reactions?

For patients with a history of HR to contrast media, the EAACI guidelines10 recommend skin prick and intradermal testing for both the suspected and alternative contrast agents, ideally 2 to 6months post-reaction. Negative results should be followed by a direct provocation challenge. Skin prick testing uses undiluted contrast (300-320mg/mL), while intradermal testing uses a 1:10 dilution. Various challenge protocols exist in the literature; a recent paper indicated a two-step challenge with 5 and 30mL dose separated by 15minutes can successfully identify patients potentially having an IgE-mediated reaction to contrast media.105 As outlined above, the evidence supporting various testing protocols are weak and unclear. Accurate positive predictive value assessments are difficult due to the rarity of severe reactions and limited patient reexposure data in patients with positive testing. An exhaustive ocular examination to assess abnormalities of the conjunctiva, cornea, and tear film, together with collection of the patient’s clinical history should always be the first steps. Allergen-specific IgE response should be ascertained: the skin prick test (SPT), along with in vitro specific IgE measurement, is still considered the gold standard for this, although if the relationship between allergen exposure and ocular signs and symptoms is not clear, a conjunctival allergen provocation test may also be performed [1, 17]. ### Over‑the‑counter Medications

One important problem is that patients with ocular allergic disease often self-medicate; they purchase OTC medications and fail to seek help even when those therapies are ineffective [22, 23]. In one study [18], self-treatment measures were the first step taken by 56% of patients diagnosed with AC. Many OTC drugs are topical vasoconstrictors or decongestants that have limited efficacy in OA, as they do not treat the underlying cause of the disease [7]. Conversely, the use and overuse of OTC products may lead to adverse effects such as rebound vasodilation [23]. Furthermore, BAK is a very

common preservative in these solutions – present in over 70% of OTC eye drops – that, as mentioned, has the potential to induce ocular toxicity and exacerbate ocular surface damage [7]. ## Is There Room for Improvement in the Management of AC? AC continues to be an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease [7]. Considering the need for differential diagnosis, a multidisciplinary approach involving allergists, general practitioners, otolaryngologists, and eye care specialists is advisable [1, 17]. It should be borne in mind that in many settings, allergic conjunctivitis patients are often seen in primary care and, when referred to a specialist, those with SAC symptoms are usually referred to the allergist, while patients with PAC are more often referred to the ophthalmologist for differential diagnosis [1].

Narrative summary: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives. SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease. First-line pharmacological therapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and dual-action agents, with recent additions like bilastine 0.6 mg/ml (preservative-free, once daily, co-formulated with hyaluronic acid) and cetirizine 2.4 mg/ml. However, many older products contain benzalkonium chloride (BAK), a preservative that disrupts the epithelial barrier and may promote dry eye. The review tabulates approved multi-dose formulations, detailing their excipients, dosing, and preservative content. For instance, levocabastine, emedastine, and several dual-action agents contain BAK at varying concentrations, while preservative-free single-dose options exist for ketotifen, olopatadine, and azelastine. Topical vasoconstrictors and NSAIDs are discouraged due to limited efficacy and adverse effects, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases under ophthalmological supervision. Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. Condition or topic: Ocular allergy, specifically allergic conjunctivitis (seasonal and perennial)

Clinical background: Ocular allergy represents a set of often underappreciated immune-mediated inflammatory conditions affecting the anterior eye surface, encompassing various clinical presentations in both children and adults. Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common form and is sub-classified into seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and perennial allergic conjunctivitis depending on whether the triggering aeroallergen is seasonal or present year-round; grass pollen is the most frequent sensitizer in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, whereas dust mites and animal dander predominate in perennial allergic conjunctivitis. The prevalence of ocular allergy has been rising globally for decades, with seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis affecting between 14% and up to 45% of the general population depending on geographic area. Despite this, allergic conjunctivitis remains underdiagnosed and undertreated—only 10% of affected individuals seek medical attention, with most self-managing using over-the-counter products and non-pharmacological remedies. Ocular allergy frequently coexists with other ocular disorders such as infections and dry eye disease, markedly impairs quality of life, and imposes a substantial economic burden. Management encompasses preventive, non-pharmacological, and pharmacological strategies. First-line pharmacotherapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and agents with dual activity, while corticosteroids and immunomodulators are reserved for severe keratoconjunctivitis. Because many patients receive topical treatments for prolonged periods, the short- and long-term safety and ocular surface tolerability of these preparations are critical; certain excipients in ophthalmic solutions can disrupt the epithelial barrier and tear film, potentially leading to dry eye or exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. The review aims to collate current evidence on these therapeutic options.

Narrative summary: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives. SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease. The review tabulates approved multi-dose formulations, detailing their excipients, dosing, and preservative content. Topical vasoconstrictors and NSAIDs are discouraged due to limited efficacy and adverse effects, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases under ophthalmological supervision. Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. ## Update on Topical Pharmacological Treatment

The recommended management approach for acute and chronic forms of OA starts with allergen identification, followed by non-pharmacological treatments (allergen avoidance and hygiene measures), progressing finally to pharmacological treatment [1]. Etiological treatment with various forms of immunotherapy can be offered under the guidance of specialists [1, 19]; when specific sensitization is the main cause of ocular allergy, allergen immunotherapy should be considered, as it has shown to be effective in reducing total and individual ocular symptoms of SAC and PAC [1, 17, 19]. The aim of pharmacological treatment in OA is to provide control and relief of signs and symptoms [1]. According to guidelines and consensus documents, topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers or double-action drugs should be the first line of treatment for the management of SAC and PAC [1, 4, 17, 19]. Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with suspected anaphylaxis, based on acute onset of symptoms involving skin/mucosal tissue plus respiratory compromise, cardiovascular instability, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or acute hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after known allergen exposure.
  Decision rules:
    - Immediately remove suspected trigger if possible (e.g., discontinue drug infusion).
    - Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin.
    - Call for emergency medical services simultaneously.
    - Inject epinephrine (adrenaline) intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh).
    - Position patient: supine unless respiratory distress (then sitting); if pregnant, left lateral semi-recumbent; if unconscious, recovery position.
    - Repeat intramuscular epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms refractory.
    - If respiratory distress, administer high-flow oxygen (100% non-rebreather mask) and consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway obstruction or inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists for bronchoconstriction (not as substitute for epinephrine).
    - If cardiovascular instability, establish IV access with wide-bore cannula, give IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg crystalloid), and consider IV epinephrine infusion under expert monitoring if refractory.
    - Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm, and respiratory status frequently; observe for biphasic reaction (at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions).
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer 0.01 mg/kg body weight (maximum 0.5 mg per dose) into the antero-lateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed to control symptoms.
      Duration cycles: Until symptoms resolve; may require multiple doses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Intravenous epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion
      Summary: For anaphylaxis refractory to repeated intramuscular epinephrine. Must be administered by experienced personnel with cardiac monitoring, preferably as an infusion via pump. Various low-dose protocols exist (e.g., Brown et al. protocol).
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis with ongoing cardiovascular or respiratory compromise despite appropriate intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: Consider for upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal edema) as an adjunct to intramuscular epinephrine.
      Conditions for use: Signs of upper airway obstruction (stridor). Not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol)
      Summary: Adjuvant for bronchoconstriction symptoms after epinephrine administration.
      Conditions for use: Persistent bronchospasm despite epinephrine.
    - Name: H1-antihistamines (second-generation oral or first-generation parenteral)
      Summary: May help relieve cutaneous symptoms (e.g., urticaria, pruritus). Limited role; should not delay epinephrine administration. Parenteral first-generation agents (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, clemastine) available; rapid IV administration can cause hypotension. Some guidelines consider them third-line.
      Conditions for use: Symptomatic relief of skin manifestations only, after epinephrine.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids (e.g., intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone)
      Summary: Historically used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, especially in asthmatic patients. Increasing evidence questions benefit; routine use controversial.
      Conditions for use: Consider in moderate-severe anaphylaxis, particularly with asthma, after epinephrine. Not for acute rescue.
    - Name: Glucagon
      Summary: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis not optimally responding to epinephrine, especially those on beta-blockers. Evidence limited.
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blockers.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Intravenous bolus epinephrine
      Reason: Risk of fatal arrhythmias; intravenous route should not be used for initial treatment and only as infusion under expert monitoring.
    - Name: Antihistamines as first-line therapy
      Reason: Do not replace epinephrine; they have a limited role and may delay life-saving epinephrine administration.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids as sole acute treatment
      Reason: No evidence of benefit in acute anaphylaxis management; routine use is controversial and may be harmful.

    - Timepoint: Throughout acute management
      Method: Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status.
      Interpretation: Reassess for resolution of symptoms or signs of biphasic reaction. Biphasic reactions may occur within 6-12 hours after initial reaction.

      Interpretation: Ensure no recurrence before discharge; educate patient on risk of biphasic reaction and indications to return.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with suspected anaphylaxis, based on acute onset of symptoms involving skin/mucosal tissue plus respiratory compromise, cardiovascular instability, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or acute hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after known allergen exposure.
  Decision rules:
    - Immediately remove suspected trigger if possible (e.g., discontinue drug infusion).
    - Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin.
    - Call for emergency medical services simultaneously.
    - Inject epinephrine (adrenaline) intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh).
    - Position patient: supine unless respiratory distress (then sitting); if pregnant, left lateral semi-recumbent; if unconscious, recovery position.
    - Repeat intramuscular epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms refractory.
    - If respiratory distress, administer high-flow oxygen (100% non-rebreather mask) and consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway obstruction or inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists for bronchoconstriction (not as substitute for epinephrine).
    - If cardiovascular instability, establish IV access with wide-bore cannula, give IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg crystalloid), and consider IV epinephrine infusion under expert monitoring if refractory.
    - Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm, and respiratory status frequently; observe for biphasic reaction (at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions).
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer 0.01 mg/kg body weight (maximum 0.5 mg per dose) into the antero-lateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed to control symptoms.
      Duration cycles: Until symptoms resolve; may require multiple doses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Intravenous epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion
      Summary: For anaphylaxis refractory to repeated intramuscular epinephrine. Must be administered by experienced personnel with cardiac monitoring, preferably as an infusion via pump. Various low-dose protocols exist (e.g., Brown et al. protocol).
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis with ongoing cardiovascular or respiratory compromise despite appropriate intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: Consider for upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal edema) as an adjunct to intramuscular epinephrine.
      Conditions for use: Signs of upper airway obstruction (stridor). Not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol)
      Summary: Adjuvant for bronchoconstriction symptoms after epinephrine administration.
      Conditions for use: Persistent bronchospasm despite epinephrine.
    - Name: H1-antihistamines (second-generation oral or first-generation parenteral)
      Summary: May help relieve cutaneous symptoms (e.g., urticaria, pruritus). Limited role; should not delay epinephrine administration. Parenteral first-generation agents (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, clemastine) available; rapid IV administration can cause hypotension. Some guidelines consider them third-line.
      Conditions for use: Symptomatic relief of skin manifestations only, after epinephrine.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids (e.g., intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone)
      Summary: Historically used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, especially in asthmatic patients. Increasing evidence questions benefit; routine use controversial.
      Conditions for use: Consider in moderate-severe anaphylaxis, particularly with asthma, after epinephrine. Not for acute rescue.
    - Name: Glucagon
      Summary: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis not optimally responding to epinephrine, especially those on beta-blockers. Evidence limited.
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blockers.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Intravenous bolus epinephrine
      Reason: Risk of fatal arrhythmias; intravenous route should not be used for initial treatment and only as infusion under expert monitoring.
    - Name: Antihistamines as first-line therapy
      Reason: Do not replace epinephrine; they have a limited role and may delay life-saving epinephrine administration.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids as sole acute treatment
      Reason: No evidence of benefit in acute anaphylaxis management; routine use is controversial and may be harmful.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Throughout acute management
      Method: Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status.
      Interpretation: Reassess for resolution of symptoms or signs of biphasic reaction. Biphasic reactions may occur within 6-12 hours after initial reaction.
    - Timepoint: After initial treatment and stabilization
      Method: Observation period of at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions or those requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
      Interpretation: Ensure no recurrence before discharge; educate patient on risk of biphasic reaction and indications to return.
  Supportive care:
    - High flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) for respiratory distress or patients receiving repeated epinephrine.
    - Intravenous access with wide-bore cannula (14 or 16 gauge in adults).
    - Intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) for cardiovascular instability.
    - Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous cardiac compressions if indicated.
    - Positioning: supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress); left lateral semi-recumbent if pregnant; recovery position if unconscious.
  Special considerations: Pregnant patients: position in left lateral semi-recumbent. Patients on beta-blockers: may require glucagon for refractory symptoms. Self-management: patients at risk should carry epinephrine auto-injector and have a written emergency action plan; instruct on when and how to self-administer epinephrine into the antero-lateral thigh.

  Title: Summarized barriers to school SE and potential improvement strategies

      Improvement strategies: Ensure legal immunity from liability in every state.
    Row 2:
      Barriers to school se: EDD cost
      Improvement strategies: Use free or low-cost school EDD programs from EDD manufacturer and advocate for more similar programs from additional pharmaceutical companies. Advocate for targeted state funding to school districts.
    Row 3:
      Barriers to school se: EDD access factors
      Improvement strategies: Advocate for legislation to increase EDD supply at stabilized cost. Expand EDD generic options. Increase awareness of physicians and nurses regarding all EDD options. Work to address EDD shortages. Advocate for 1 EDD injector pack option.
    Row 4:
      Barriers to school se: Lack of SNs or inadequate quantity of SNs per student and school needs
      Improvement strategies: Increase number of SNs in school districts with aim of at least 1 per school. Clarify accurate SN educational preparedness, scope of practice, and role. Increase recruitment, retainment, and available funding for full-time SNs.
    Row 5:
      Barriers to school se: Absence of or inconsistent quality of comprehensive evidence-based anaphylaxis training of school UAP
      Improvement strategies: Increase awareness of available free or low-cost peer-reviewed training materials. Promote understanding of SN competency as leaders in providing comprehensive anaphylaxis management education to UAP.
    Row 6:
      Barriers to school se: Obstacles to delegating medication administration to school UAP by SNs
      Improvement strategies: Promote legal ability for SNs to delegate medication administration to school UAP. Advocate for at least 1 full-time SN in every school building. Ensure incentives to increase quantity of willing school UAP to be SN trained and supervised for medication administration.
    Row 7:
      Barriers to school se: Licensed prescriber hesitancy or absence of sufficient quantity of willing licensed prescribers for school SE
      Improvement strategies: Improve quantity of willing licensed prescribers by using school or district physicians when present and/or local physicians, including those from local health departments. Advocate for state legislation as needed to require state department of health designate a default prescribing physician if no willing local physicians are available. Provide accurate information on immunity from liability per state laws and regulations. Ensure availability of toolkits containing current resources and materials to facilitate licensed prescriber ease in ordering school SE.
    Row 8:
      Barriers to school se: Legislative challenges
      Improvement strategies: Improve legislative support for mandated school SE in all states.
    Row 9:
      Barriers to school se: School administration and school board factors
      Improvement strategies: Provide advocacy and education to schools on merits of SE. Promote support of SNs. Counsel that ample time is needed for provision of effective anaphylaxis education to school personnel.
    Row 10:
      Barriers to school se: Health care provider factors
      Improvement strategies: Use collaborative team approach to school anaphylaxis management with family/student, SN, school staff, and student’s clinical physicians and nurses. Provision by clinical teams of current and complete student-specific anaphylaxis action plans and school medication forms to patients/families and schools at start of academic year and as needed. Educate schools on the need for SE for students with no prior diagnosis of anaphylaxis.
    Row 11:
      Barriers to school se: Family and student factors
      Improvement strategies: Provision of comprehensive culturally competent anaphylaxis education to students/families by SNs and student’s clinical team of physicians and nurses. Delivery of all necessary completed medical and medication forms to schools by family/student.

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development

Used appropriately, the D&I sciences provide important tools to promote EBP and health equity as well as optimization of clinical practice in allergy and immunology. Although the D&I sciences are well recognized by the NIH and have gained traction in other medical disciplines, their use in allergy and immunology has lagged.12-17 As a result, allergists and immunologists are frequently tasked to develop local protocols to deliver care that is based on new evidencewithin their individual clinical settings. Although implementation strategies are occasionally included in more recent guidelines, there is still a need to improve the implementation of EBP within the field of allergy and immunology.18-24 In this American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (AAAAI) work group report, we advocate for a greater awareness and understanding of the D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement (QI), practice improvement, health services research, and GRADE (Grades of Recommendation Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) based guideline development. We also provide examples of where the D&I sciences can improve the care of allergy and immunology patients.15,25-27 Dissemination science is the study of how information and intervention materials are distributed to a specific audience; implementation science is the scientific study of methods to promote the systematic uptake of proven clinical treatments and practices as well as organizational and management interventions into routine clinical practice.15 We refer to these fields of study together as the D&I sciences.

For example, a QI project may focus on developing an intervention to increase screening for primary immunodeficiency in primary care and work to iteratively improve the intervention using a focused plan– do–study–act (aka PDSA) cycle approach. A D&I study may approach this observed care gap differently and use a systematic approach to identify and address key factors affecting the interventions, including individual features (what are the attitudes and knowledge of frontline clinicians? ), organizational aspects (are there adequate nursing and laboratory supports and equipment? ), cultural considerations (how will we discuss this intervention in various populations? ), and financial climate (will payors restrict screening lab payments?). Specifically, the D&I sciences provide a validated, systematic approach to study the intervention itself as well outcomes relevant to successful and widespread use of the intervention, including effectiveness (is the intervention working as intended? ), reach (are we reaching the intended patient populations or clinical settings? ), fidelity (is the intervention deployed as intended? ), and sustainability (can we maintain our intervention over time? ).28-31

Another value of the D&I sciences is to develop processes to discontinue interventions of low value, such as deimplementing steroid therapy to prevent late-phase reactions in anaphylaxis. ### Concomitant Pathologies and Differential Diagnosis

Allergic conjunctivitis is often comorbid with allergic rhinitis (AR) [14]. The two disorders are so strongly and frequently associated that they are defined in most countries as

a single condition (e.g., allergic rhinoconjunctivitis) [15]. When this happens, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians or even patients as a minor problem, and therefore ocular manifestations are frequently misdiagnosed or underdiagnosed, and not properly managed [1, 16] or sub-optimally treated [10]. Therefore, when compared to AR, allergic conjunctivitis receives far less attention [7]. In many countries, most cases are diagnosed and managed by a general practitioner and rarely referred to specialists, even when other signs and symptoms suggest a systemic allergic disorder that would be more appropriately treated by a specialist [1]. Notably, the therapeutic approach of primary care physicians and eye care specialists has been discordant [1], and this is also true for allergists. In this regard, a common knowledge base such as that provided by this review may be useful to detect areas for improvement.

DED and AC coexist and show a significant clinical overlap. In fact, AC and DED are the most common ocular surface disorders, and they both have a potentially severe impact on patients’ QoL [15]. Bearing DED in mind is crucial when assessing AC as they can both be considered as conditions that predispose to or at least facilitate each other [10]. Eye itching, conjunctival redness and tear film dysfunction have been detected in both conditions, thus complicating differential diagnosis [10]. In addition, the prolonged use of some topical and systemic medications, especially eye drop formulations containing BAK as a preservative, can contribute to the development of DED.

Condition or topic: Ocular allergy, specifically allergic conjunctivitis (seasonal and perennial)

Clinical background: Ocular allergy represents a set of often underappreciated immune-mediated inflammatory conditions affecting the anterior eye surface, encompassing various clinical presentations in both children and adults. Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common form and is sub-classified into seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and perennial allergic conjunctivitis depending on whether the triggering aeroallergen is seasonal or present year-round; grass pollen is the most frequent sensitizer in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, whereas dust mites and animal dander predominate in perennial allergic conjunctivitis. The prevalence of ocular allergy has been rising globally for decades, with seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis affecting between 14% and up to 45% of the general population depending on geographic area. Despite this, allergic conjunctivitis remains underdiagnosed and undertreated—only 10% of affected individuals seek medical attention, with most self-managing using over-the-counter products and non-pharmacological remedies. Ocular allergy frequently coexists with other ocular disorders such as infections and dry eye disease, markedly impairs quality of life, and imposes a substantial economic burden. Management encompasses preventive, non-pharmacological, and pharmacological strategies. First-line pharmacotherapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and agents with dual activity, while corticosteroids and immunomodulators are reserved for severe keratoconjunctivitis. Because many patients receive topical treatments for prolonged periods, the short- and long-term safety and ocular surface tolerability of these preparations are critical; certain excipients in ophthalmic solutions can disrupt the epithelial barrier and tear film, potentially leading to dry eye or exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. The review aims to collate current evidence on these therapeutic options.

When symptoms of allergic rhinitis are present, treatment options usually include systemic antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids [1]. In this scenario, the use of second-generation systemic antihistamines, with fewer adverse events and a much better profile in terms of sedation, is recommended [4, 5, 7]. The potential of some systemic antihistamines to worsen the ocular surface due to their anticholinergic effect should be taken into account [10]. Systemic leukotriene receptor antagonists have proved to be useful in the treatment of allergic rhinitis, although less than oral antihistamines [17]; but they have a limited use for the treatment of OA [1, 24]. Topical immunomodulators such

- as calcineurin inhibitors, cyclosporine and tacrolimus, are recommended for chronic diseases of OA (vernal or atopic keratoconjunctivitis) [1, 17]. Their use depends on severity and frequency of exacerbations. Topical corticosteroids may


be used for severe forms of OA and in uncontrolled exacerbations of SAC and PAC since their use is associated with potentially significant adverse reactions [17, 25]. Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are not recommended for the treatment of SAC and PAC [17]. Many patients also require the concomitant use of lubricating eye drops to maximize control of ocular allergy symptoms [26]. Finally, in patients with severe forms of SAC and PAC, following the recommendations of the EAACI guidelines, allergen immunotherapy (AIT) should be considered a therapeutic option [19]. AIT is indicated when IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is evidenced, after first-line treatment failure, or to modify the natural course of ocular allergic disease. Systemic immunosuppressive treatment and biologic therapy may be prescribed in severe forms of OA, such as refractory vernal or atopic keratoconjunctivitis [17].

Adherence to topical ophthalmic treatment in eye conditions has been widely studied. Patient preference for an eye drop can often be a primary factor in determining the level of compliance and adherence to treatment [46]. Discomfort upon instillation (as produced by NSAIDs) and long regular dosing (as required for efficacy in treatment with mast cells stabilizers) are other causes that have been associated with a poorer treatment adherence [1]. At present, there is a large market interest in preservative-free products,

particularly for patients who need daily eye drops for long periods. Single-dose or single-use containers, which do not need preservatives [50, 54], and some multi-dose [64], preservative-free ophthalmic solutions are now available thanks to innovative device design, making it possible for patient preferences to be considered. In our experience, some patients may prefer single-dose presentations, as they find them more convenient, however a multi-dose presentation has the benefit of reducing product waste, common in single-dose eye drops. In addition, patients requiring permanent or longterm topical eye treatment, namely glaucoma, have better treatment compliance with multi-dose delivery systems [65, 66], and this may be applicable to AC. Several single-dose eye drop formulations are available for allergic conjunctivitis [50, 54], in addition to the usual BAK-containing multidose solutions, and a new preservative-free multi-dose formulation of bilastine with sodium hyaluronate has been recently approved [64].Along with the dispensation format, approaches to improving treatment adherence include treatment tolerability [67] and dosing schedules, as complex drug dosing regimens have been cited as a significant barrier to patient compliance [68, 69]. Simplifying dosing can be achieved by prescribing treatments that require once- or twice-daily dosing rather than multiple daily doses [69]. Once-daily ophthalmic medications are now available for allergic conjunctivitis [31, 37, 38], and this could foster adherence and treatment compliance.

Condition or topic: Ocular allergy, specifically allergic conjunctivitis (seasonal and perennial)

Clinical background: Ocular allergy represents a set of often underappreciated immune-mediated inflammatory conditions affecting the anterior eye surface, encompassing various clinical presentations in both children and adults. Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common form and is sub-classified into seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and perennial allergic conjunctivitis depending on whether the triggering aeroallergen is seasonal or present year-round; grass pollen is the most frequent sensitizer in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, whereas dust mites and animal dander predominate in perennial allergic conjunctivitis. The prevalence of ocular allergy has been rising globally for decades, with seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis affecting between 14% and up to 45% of the general population depending on geographic area. Despite this, allergic conjunctivitis remains underdiagnosed and undertreated—only 10% of affected individuals seek medical attention, with most self-managing using over-the-counter products and non-pharmacological remedies. Ocular allergy frequently coexists with other ocular disorders such as infections and dry eye disease, markedly impairs quality of life, and imposes a substantial economic burden. Management encompasses preventive, non-pharmacological, and pharmacological strategies. First-line pharmacotherapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and agents with dual activity, while corticosteroids and immunomodulators are reserved for severe keratoconjunctivitis. Because many patients receive topical treatments for prolonged periods, the short- and long-term safety and ocular surface tolerability of these preparations are critical; certain excipients in ophthalmic solutions can disrupt the epithelial barrier and tear film, potentially leading to dry eye or exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. The review aims to collate current evidence on these therapeutic options.

Main conclusion: The management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis should prioritize topical therapies that effectively control signs and symptoms while minimizing iatrogenic damage to the ocular surface, as many commercial formulations contain preservatives like benzalkonium chloride that can disrupt the tear film and exacerbate dry eye disease.

Narrative summary: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives. SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease. First-line pharmacological therapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and dual-action agents, with recent additions like bilastine 0.6 mg/ml (preservative-free, once daily, co-formulated with hyaluronic acid) and cetirizine 2.4 mg/ml. However, many older products contain benzalkonium chloride (BAK), a preservative that disrupts the epithelial barrier and may promote dry eye. The review tabulates approved multi-dose formulations, detailing their excipients, dosing, and preservative content. For instance, levocabastine, emedastine, and several dual-action agents contain BAK at varying concentrations, while preservative-free single-dose options exist for ketotifen, olopatadine, and azelastine. Topical vasoconstrictors and NSAIDs are discouraged due to limited efficacy and adverse effects, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases under ophthalmological supervision. Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. In summary, clinicians should select topical agents not only for their antiallergic efficacy but also for their formulation’s impact on the ocular surface, preferentially using preservative-free or low-toxicity preparations to optimize long-term safety and tolerability.

Summary Seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC) are the most frequent causes of ocular allergy (OA), and both conditions are underdiagnosed and undertreated. SAC and PAC are immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity reactions. The additional tear film disruption caused by the release of inflammatory mediators increases and exacerbates the impact of signs and symptoms and may trigger damage of the ocular surface. Comorbidities are frequent, and dry eye disease in particular must be considered. Clinical guidelines for the management of SAC and PAC recommend topical therapy with antihistamines, mast cells stabilizers or dualaction agents as first-line treatment, but care should be taken, as many medications contain other compounds that may contribute to ocular surface damage.

Introduction Ocular allergy (OA) represents a collection of ocular hypersensitivity disorders affecting the eyelid, conjunctiva and cornea. OA includes seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC), vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis (VKC and AKC) and contact blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC) (1). These clinical subtypes may be diagnosed and managed by ophthalmologists, allergists, pediatricians and rhinologists, with or without experience in managing allergies, considering clinical history and signs and symptoms, aided by in vivo and in vitro tests (1-3). Although several studies suggest a high co-morbidity of conjunctivitis and rhinitis, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians as a minor problem and sub-optimally treated. A recent survey revealed that daily treatment of OA has little concordance with current recommendations(4). Topical ocular decongestants and corticosteroids were used in the majority of cases. This was independent of the specific diagnosis of OA subtype and severity. Topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers, which

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature.

Pharmacodynamics: Propiedades farmacodinámicas

Grupo farmacoterapéutico: Antihistamínicos de uso sistémico, otros antihistamínicos de uso sistémico. Código ATC: R06AX29.

Mecanismo de acción

Bilastina es un antihistamínico no sedante y de acción prolongada, con afinidad antagonista selectiva por los receptores H1 periféricos y sin afinidad por los receptores muscarínicos. Tras la administración de una dosis única bilastina inhibió durante 24 horas las reacciones cutáneas de habón y eritema inducidas por histamina. 

Eficacia clínica y seguridad

Los estudios de eficacia y seguridad se realizaron con la formulación en comprimidos, a la que se ha demostrado que bilastina 20 mg comprimidos bucodispersables es bioequivalente. En ensayos clínicos realizados en pacientes adultos y adolescentes con rinoconjuntivitis alérgica (estacional y perenne), bilastina administrada en una única dosis diaria de 20 mg durante 14-28 días fue eficaz para aliviar los síntomas, tales como estornudos, rinorrea, picor nasal, congestión nasal, picor ocular, lagrimeo y enrojecimiento ocular. Bilastina controló los síntomas de forma eficaz durante 24 horas. En dos ensayos clínicos realizados en pacientes con urticaria crónica idiopática, bilastina administrada en una única dosis diaria de 20 mg durante 28 días fue eficaz para aliviar la intensidad del prurito y el número y tamaño de los habones, así como el malestar de los pacientes derivado de la urticaria. Los pacientes obtuvieron una mejoría en la calidad del sueño y en la calidad de vida. En los ensayos clínicos realizados con bilastina no se observó ninguna prolongación del intervalo QTc ni ningún otro efecto cardiovascular clínicamente relevantes, incluso a dosis hasta 200 mg diarios (10 veces la dosis terapéutica) durante 7 días en 9 sujetos o incluso cuando se administraron de forma concomitante inhibidores de P-gp, tales como ketoconazol (24 sujetos) y eritromicina (24 sujetos). Además, se ha llevado a cabo un estudio “thorough QT” en 30 voluntarios. En los ensayos clínicos controlados realizados con la dosis recomendada, 20 mg una vez al día, el perfil de seguridad de bilastina sobre el SNC fue similar al placebo y la incidencia de somnolencia no fue estadísticamente diferente a placebo. Bilastina a dosis hasta 40 mg cada día no afectó al rendimiento psicomotor en los ensayos clínicos y no afectó a la capacidad de conducción en un estudio estándar de conducción. La eficacia y seguridad de bilastina en los pacientes de edad avanzada (≥ 65 años) incluidos en los estudios de fase II y III no mostraron diferencias con respecto a pacientes más jóvenes. Un estudio post autorización con 146 pacientes de edad avanzada no mostró diferencias en el perfil de seguridad con respecto a la población adulta. 

Población pediátrica

En el desarrollo clínico se incluyeron adolescentes (de 12 a 17 años). Durante los ensayos clínicos 128 adolescentes recibieron bilastina (81 en ensayos doble ciego de rinoconjuntivitis alérgica). Otros 116 adolescentes fueron asignados al azar a comparadores activos o placebo. No se observaron diferencias en eficacia ni en seguridad entre adultos y adolescentes. De acuerdo a las directrices, la eficacia probada en adultos y adolescentes se puede extrapolar a niños, habiéndose demostrado que la exposición sistémica de 10 mg de bilastina en niños de 2 a 11 años de edad con un peso corporal mínimo de 15 kg es equivalente a la exposición de 20 mg de bilastina en adultos (ver sección 5.2). La extrapolación de datos de adultos y adolescentes se considera apropiada para este medicamento dado que la fisiopatología de la rinoconjuntivitis alérgica y la urticaria es la misma para todos los grupos de edad. En un ensayo clínico controlado de 12 semanas con niños de 2 a 11 años de edad (509 niños en total, 260 tratados con 10 mg de bilastina: 58 de 2 a <6 años de edad, 105 de 6 a <9 años de edad y 97 de 9 a <12 años de edad; y 249 tratados con placebo: 58 de 2 a <6 años de edad, 95 de 6 a <9 años de edad y 96 de 9 a <12 años de edad), a la dosis pediátrica recomendada de 10 mg una vez al día, el perfil de seguridad de bilastina (n = 260) fue similar a placebo (n = 249), con reacciones adversas a medicamentos observados en 5,8% y 8,0% de los pacientes que tomaron 10 mg de bilastina y placebo, respectivamente. Durante este estudio, ambos grupos, bilastina 10 mg y placebo, mostraron una ligera disminución en las puntuaciones de somnolencia y sedación en el Cuestionario de Sueño Pediátrico, sin diferencias estadísticamente significativas entre los grupos de tratamiento. En estos niños de 2-11 años de edad no se detectaron diferencias significativas en QTc tras la administración de 10 mg de bilastina diaria en comparación con placebo. Los cuestionarios de Calidad de Vida específicos para niños con rinoconjuntivitis alérgica o urticaria crónica mostraron un incremento general en las puntuaciones tras 12 semanas sin diferencia estadísticamente significativa entre los grupos de bilastina y placebo. La población total de 509 niños incluyó: 479 sujetos con rinoconjuntivitis alérgica y 30 sujetos diagnosticados de urticaria crónica. 260 niños recibieron bilastina, 252 (96,9%) para rinoconjuntivitis alérgica y 8 (3,1%) para la urticaria crónica. Por analogía, 249 niños recibieron placebo, 227 (91,2%) para rinoconjuntivitis alérgica y 22 (8,8%) para la urticaria crónica. La Agencia Europea de Medicamentos ha eximido de la obligación de presentar los resultados de los ensayos realizados con bilastina en todos los grupos de la población pediátrica menores de 2 años de edad (ver sección 4.2 para consultar la información sobre el uso en la población pediátrica).
